posts.content:
I have had the opportunity to engage with several policy makers on the topic of Auto PLI excluding startups and I just can’t believe that they would think so!

Over the last decade, the electric two wheeler ecosystem in India has evolved through contributions from both incumbents and electric first companies. Many of these startups invested early in product, software, power electronics, and localisation, often without the cushion of legacy scale. In doing so, they have pushed the boundaries and pulled in the competition to together build a competitive but a very vibrant and dynamic EV market.

Today in many many markets it is the ‘new age EV companies’ that are industry leaders in not just innovation and tech, but in absolute volumes and market shares. Aligned with the PLI’s vision, it is these ‘startups and new age EV companies’ that are investing hundred, even thousands of crores in most new manufacturing capacities for EVs. For example at Ather we have already employed more than 4000 people directly and tens of thousands indirectly in our channels and supply chains. We have invested thousands of crores in RnD and direct capex and on top of this we are now investing 2000 crores in our new green field facility in Maharasthra. This is literally what PLI was hoping as an outcome and is being realized by a non-PLI holder, against all odds.

And most crucially, they are doing all this while also investing heavily in R&D and domestic value addition (DVA). DVA benchmarks are similar across PLI and non PLI players so it would be wrong to assume that startups don’t lead DVA requirements. These companies have consistently pushed deeper on indigenous development, building capabilities that are at par with, and in some cases ahead of, the broader industry.

An EV policy architecture that defines champions primarily through legacy scale, not even scale within the EV industry, can create an unintended imbalance. It places emerging EV manufacturers at a 13 to 16 percent cost disadvantage at a stage where they are continuing to invest heavily in capability building. Over time, this will influence how the market evolves, even as the goal is to build both scale and future ready capability. 

In this train of EV industry if legacy businesses are the bogeys, startups and new age companies are the engine. You cannot take the engine out of the equation and hope for the bogeys to move forward themselves.

If India’s ambition is to lead in electric mobility, policy needs to recognise where innovation and capability are being built. Much of the work around indigenous platforms, battery systems, software, and domestic value addition is happening within electric first companies, and they will continue to set global benchmarks in design and technology.

What is needed is calibration of PLI, not overhaul. More flexible eligibility, aligned with localisation and R&D intensity, can help ensure we are building long term capability, not just near term scale.

Future of all interfaces on a two wheeler - voice!

We have been excited about it for a long time. Ather Energy pretty much invented the concept of touch screens on 2Ws (being the first to do that on a production bike), and we continue to invest heavily into capabilities and feature sets on it.

But even as we push the envelope on that front (almost half of our vehicles today ship with a touch TFT and 100% ship with on-board compute and connectivity) we believe the future could very well be one that does not need you to glance at the display at all.

Using LLMs and natural language processing and bundling that inside our smart helmets (Halo) we believe that being able to ‘just tell’ your scooter what you want can be super intuitive.

In fact, far more intuitive than stationary applications like mobile phones, laptops etc. On a scooter you can’t operate touch while riding, and we would rather have you glance as little as possible when in heavy traffic or at high speeds. Being able to just tell your Ather what you want, especially inside the cocoon of your helmet (or on any Bluetooth headset really), is a significant tech and experience upgrade for riders:

Navigation:
“Take me to Nandi Hills,”
“Navigate home,”
“Let’s go to Cubbon Park,”
“How far is the nearest charger?”
“ETA to jaljog choraha?”
"Time to stadium circle?"

Vehicle Settings:
“Decrease brightness,” or “Maximum brightness,”
“Change Traction control to Rain,”
“Magic twist, High,”
“Share my live location.”

Calls:
“Call Rohit” - This is fully integrated with your existing contact list.

Media controls:
“Play the next song”
“Pause”

We unveiled it last year and have finally rolled out Voice on Ather to all our Gen 3 and above customers now. Do give it a try!

Voice today is just the starting point. We believe we can build a ton of experiences for our riders on top of this capability.
Next upgrade (soon): your Ather will talk and recommend things to you. Alerts, suggestions, feedback - proactively.

🚨 India’s auto PLI (Production-linked incentive) scheme was designed to create global champion OEMs (Original Equipment Manufacturers). The ambition is not in question. 

But the recent The Economic Times report quoting a government official off-the-record, suggesting that PLI is not meant for startups is surprising.

Here’s the reality and fallout: companies like Ather Energy, River and Euler Motors who took an early electric-first bet, invested in R&D, built local IP, and validated the model, find themselves locked out of these incentives. Excluding such players is counter-intuitive. 

Plus, this does not seem aligned with the Hon’ble Prime Minister’s Startup India vision, which has fostered the emergence of several high-growth startups and unicorns by empowering new-age companies to build and innovate in India.

The argument that PLI was never meant for startups doesn’t hold up on scrutiny either. The scheme’s newer Non-Automotive category includes players with zero revenue and no prior experience. So the question writes itself: who actually needs policy support more?

The current eligibility thresholds: Rs 10,000 crore in revenue, Rs 3,000 crore in fixed assets end up excluding startups. In essence, they filter out innovation. 

Research shows these startups are already operating at a 13–16% cost disadvantage compared to PLI beneficiaries. A recent Parliamentary Standing Committee report has flagged the same gap.

The fix isn’t complicated. A dedicated window within the existing Auto PLI scheme, with eligibility criteria that recognise localisation, innovation, and early investment, not just scale, would go a long way.

There is still time to get this right.

At Startup Policy Forum, we have been closely engaging with policymakers on this issue and will continue to advocate for a more equitable and forward-looking EV policy framework.

posts.content:
Culture is not in the coffee/office decor; it's in the way people experience everyday work - Part 1

A friend had once advised me that companies typically change a few times culturally and the simplest way to track these changes is org size. You see a significant change at 60-80 folks, then again at around 300 and then finally around 2000 people. 

He advised me of this in 2017, when Ather Energy had just crossed 300 people and there were a lot of changes afoot. Why do companies change at these sizes? Most likely because additional layers come in place which changes how well communication rolls- both from founders to teams and feedback from teams to founders.

Instead of simply rolling out a form to check employee satisfaction, we realized it was time to actively start discussing our ways of working—essentially, our culture. Culture is not in the coffee, it's not in the office decor or the services that we offer; it is really in the way people experience everyday work. We figured what we’ll instead do is actually have structured conversations with different cohorts of team members, document everybody’s feedback and share their observations as well as proposed changes with the entire org. 

We went about it quite methodically the 1st time itself. Our team came up with a framework for this - Culture Conversations. The cohorts engaged were quite varied, including those from the first 50 employees to the most recent 50, women-only groups, new graduates, etc. All conversations followed a structured format, were documented anonymously, and then were used to drive insights. 

What did we change at each step of the organization?
The 1st edition of Culture Conversations happened in 2017, around the 300 people mark for us. And the insight was the need to clearly put down our value system so that it could spread easily through the fast expanding system. The obvious culture had become less clear, esp now that lateral hiring was picking pace. 
We called our values - Think As A Species™ , a framework which pushes for deep collaboration and long term thinking.

We've repeated these conversations almost every 18 months since then. The next two lots were reasonably mild in terms of feedback since the org didn’t feel that different in comparison to the previous stage, since the organization size hadn't changed that much.

The 2nd edition of the Culture Conversations concluded with us doubling down on our values. We restructured the org heavily towards a cross-functional way of working with a move towards small ‘pods’ or ‘swimlanes’ as we call them, to drive faster daily execution and better collaboration. 

By the time of the 3rd edition, Ather was nearing 1000 people and the biggest feedback was the need for more context. A monthly company-wide all hands was no longer sufficient for everybody to ask questions or understand the nuances of their OKRs and their goals. So, we worked towards increasing the frequency and forums of communication across all levels.

posts.content:
At Ather Energy, we have a credo we live by - Think As A Species™ (TAAS). It’s not just a tagline; it’s how we operate.

Building a great company isn’t just about making great products - that is the easy part. The harder challenge is building a culture that creates a lasting impact. TAAS has shaped how we work. It is how we zoom out from short-term wins and focus on what we believe moves the whole industry forward. It’s why we’ve never just optimized for Ather - we try to optimize for the industry. 

Take EV charging for instance. The easy route? Patent our connector, lock it down, and make the market adapt. Instead, we worked with regulators and the industry to create LECCS (Light Electric Combined Charging System), standardizing charging for two and three-wheelers. This meant more interoperability, shared infrastructure, and possibly a better experience for EV owners. It wasn’t the obvious choice, but it was the right one.

This thinking isn’t just for big industry moves. It’s how we operate internally, too. 
There are no silos, no lone rockstars. Problems get solved across teams and not just within departments. That’s why we built swimlanes, which are cross-functional teams that cut through hierarchies. This structure eliminates bottlenecks, speeds up decisions, and creates real ownership.

Whether it's scaling production, expanding Ather Grid, or launching new features, the approach stays the same. Engineers, designers, supply chain teams, business leads - everyone in the same room, iterating and solving together. Because no single person has all the answers, but together, we figure it out.

And since we build most of our components in-house, we can move faster, solve problems at the root, and introduce industry-firsts. Tighter integration means better coordination and quicker iteration, allowing us to build not just a great product, but a solid EV ecosystem.

Why does it work? Because when people see the bigger picture and understand the ‘why’, alignment happens naturally. That’s why we over-communicate context, set shared goals, and keep decision-making distributed. Teams don’t just execute; they shape the outcome.

That’s TAAS. That’s how we’ve built over the years. And as we scale, we’ll make sure this ethos stays at the core of everything we do.

#SPFImpact: One of the founding pillars of Startup Policy Forum has been to champion a level-playing field for startups through fair and progressive policy frameworks. 

The government’s Production-Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme has been a major catalyst for strengthening India’s manufacturing, encouraging domestic production and helping companies scale globally. 

However, many startups missed out on the Auto PLI benefits due to eligibility thresholds that did not fully account for the realities of these emerging manufacturers.

Our members including Ather Energy and River are at the forefront of India’s EV story. Yet, despite their innovation DNA and manufacturing scale and commitment, they have not been able to reap the PLI benefits.

Over the past year, SPF has worked closely with several government stakeholders to highlight this gap and advocate revisiting these eligibility thresholds under the Auto PLI scheme. We believe this level playing field is needed so that new-age companies can meaningfully contribute towards the vision of turning India into a global EV manufacturing hub.

‼️ On Wednesday, the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry tabled a report in Rajya Sabha that acknowledges this ground reality and proposes important course corrections: 

➡️ Key Observations of Parliamentary Panel 

🔹Current eligibility threholds may prevent EV startups from participating
🔹 Need flexible criteria especially for the e2W sector
🔹 Frequent downward revisions of budgets suggest overestimated allocations or slower implementation of schemes
 
➡️ Recommendations of Parliamentary Panel 

🔹Set up high-level mechanism to track capacity commissioning, sales growth and certification
🔹 Resolve spector-specific challenges such as eligibility rules that exclude domestic startups

This represents a small but very significant sign of progress for us as the report echoes what SPF has been consistently highlighting in conversations with policymakers.

As next steps, we look forward to  working with relevant stakeholders to take forward the proposals from the Parliamentary panel. These reforms will ensure the PLI scheme delivers on its intended goal and maximises its impact by including all relevant and deserving players of the EV ecosystem.

posts.content:
Culture is not in the coffee/office decor; it's in the way people experience everyday work - Part 2

Finally, we just concluded the latest version - Culture conversation 4.0.

This time the org is nearing 2000 people and almost predictably the feedback was the strongest this time after several years.

Key concerns this time have been around:
- Too many short term conversations and much operational drudgery 
- Org growth is creating a sense of distance from leadership and managers pulling in different directions
- Lack of celebration and recognition

A lot of this I can trace to us more than doubling our permanent headcount in less than 12 months in FY23. Amod Malviya (आमोद मालवीय, ಆಮೋದ ಮಾಲವೀಯ) at Udaan had warned me about this many years back but the operational pressure made us anyway do it and the culture paid a price for it. Rapid headcount growth after a certain stage makes it impossible to assimilate people well, creates too many new folks around who can’t get enough ‘wisdom’ conversations from the old folks to keep some cultural stability + it inevitably puts recruitment systems under pressure which generally means something’s got to give. Even if you keep the competence bar the same, there is still a cultural downgrade in selection.

The other reason is the massive growth followed by a near complete strategy change suddenly last year owing to the sudden subsidy changes. It messes with the communication channels and apart from a small group of folks very close to the founders, most people feel that they are on an ever changing see-saw with no rhythm or rhyme.

On the good side, people love how accessible everybody still remains at Ather, how customer-centric the org still is, and how logical most conversations still are and generally first-principles based thinking it is.

I am sure that this culture conversations feedback will need a bunch of work. The essence still remains but fixing the chaos of last year won’t be a quick fix, esp at this size. 

But then, we’ve always focused on the long-term game. And investing to build an organization that grows and evolves is actually quite natural to Swapnil Jain and me. Part of the reason I am sharing this publicly is to hammer the point as to how important this topic is to us. Watch this thread for an update on how things pan out next year.
#WorkCulture

repost.content:
Culture is not in the coffee/office decor; it's in the way people experience everyday work - Part 1

A friend had once advised me that companies typically change a few times culturally and the simplest way to track these changes is org size. You see a significant change at 60-80 folks, then again at around 300 and then finally around 2000 people. 

He advised me of this in 2017, when Ather Energy had just crossed 300 people and there were a lot of changes afoot. Why do companies change at these sizes? Most likely because additional layers come in place which changes how well communication rolls- both from founders to teams and feedback from teams to founders.

Instead of simply rolling out a form to check employee satisfaction, we realized it was time to actively start discussing our ways of working—essentially, our culture. Culture is not in the coffee, it's not in the office decor or the services that we offer; it is really in the way people experience everyday work. We figured what we’ll instead do is actually have structured conversations with different cohorts of team members, document everybody’s feedback and share their observations as well as proposed changes with the entire org. 

We went about it quite methodically the 1st time itself. Our team came up with a framework for this - Culture Conversations. The cohorts engaged were quite varied, including those from the first 50 employees to the most recent 50, women-only groups, new graduates, etc. All conversations followed a structured format, were documented anonymously, and then were used to drive insights. 

What did we change at each step of the organization?
The 1st edition of Culture Conversations happened in 2017, around the 300 people mark for us. And the insight was the need to clearly put down our value system so that it could spread easily through the fast expanding system. The obvious culture had become less clear, esp now that lateral hiring was picking pace. 
We called our values - Think As A Species™ , a framework which pushes for deep collaboration and long term thinking.

We've repeated these conversations almost every 18 months since then. The next two lots were reasonably mild in terms of feedback since the org didn’t feel that different in comparison to the previous stage, since the organization size hadn't changed that much.

The 2nd edition of the Culture Conversations concluded with us doubling down on our values. We restructured the org heavily towards a cross-functional way of working with a move towards small ‘pods’ or ‘swimlanes’ as we call them, to drive faster daily execution and better collaboration. 

By the time of the 3rd edition, Ather was nearing 1000 people and the biggest feedback was the need for more context. A monthly company-wide all hands was no longer sufficient for everybody to ask questions or understand the nuances of their OKRs and their goals. So, we worked towards increasing the frequency and forums of communication across all levels.

#MondayMusings: ⁩”Buland Bharat ki Buland Tasveer” - Sixteen years ago, I sat down with Rahul Bajaj and Rajiv Bajaj for one of the most memorable interviews of my TV career.

It was a defining moment for #India, and the Bajaj family. 

Rajiv, the young heir, was determined to end the production of the iconic Bajaj scooter and pivot to motorcycles. 

It’s a shift his father Rahul resisted, voicing his disappointment on national TV in his characteristic outspoken style, yet ensuring he’s passing on the decision-making baton effectively to the next generation. 

That candid exchange captured India's profound bond with the scooter. It also spotlighted the dynamics of generational change in family businesses.

The Bajaj Chetak defined an era, from decade-long waiting lists to Rahul Bajaj's unforgettable quip in the interview that "marriages wouldn't happen in India without a Bajaj scooter demanded in dowry."

🚀🛵 Cut to today: India still moves on two wheels, but electric vehicles (EVs) are reshaping the road ahead. 

Bajaj has re-entered scooters with EVs, yet innovation surges from bold startups like Ather Energy and River, new entrants that are rewriting rules, grabbing market share, and forcing legacy players to catch up.

Ather's rise is electric! When Avantika Gode and I toured their Bengaluru tech center, we were super impressed to witness the innovation stack and global benchmarks being set by this IIT Madras-incubated startup, from battery tech to smart charging.

As an observer of India’s economic landscape over the years, it's fascinating to see how trailblazing companies are redefining traditional sectors. 

This startup-driven dynamism demands bold policy, or at minimum, a true level-playing field. Yet even the most well-intentioned policies can have unintended consequences.

Take the Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme: Rigid criteria exclude many EV two-wheeler innovators, burdening startups with cost disadvantages while favouring incumbents, what Ather founder Tarun Mehta calls a "policy disability."

This hampers true pioneers, risks stalling India's EV ambitions, and cedes export dominance to China.

To fuel New India's energy, where startups challenge giants and propel us globally, policy must be bias-free, and innovation-first. 

At the Startup Policy Forum, we will continue working with stakeholders to try and address such anomalies. 

Meanwhile, the Bajaj jingle still stirs immense nostalgia. At the same time it also reminds us that Buland Bharat is accelerating, faster than we know it.

repost.content:
When we started with the Ather 450, we focused sharply on performance and sportiness. Unabashedly. With our second product line, Ather Rizta, we wanted to focus on a larger market segment- family scooters. We wanted to deliver strongly on family-oriented needs ie comfort, convenience and safety. Interestingly, there was no EV positioned sharply as a wholesome family scooter. And that was the opportunity. 

So, it started with a simple question: What is it that a family needs in a scooter? We recognized that a scooter often isn’t just one person’s ride. It’s not seen as “mine”—it's seen as "ours." We needed something that was spacious enough for groceries, easy to ride and handle, comfortable for all ages and brings a whole lot of convenience to the table. And so, the Rizta was born and adorned with a host of features such as a large seat, Atherstack updates such as Whatsapp on the dashboard, ride assist features like AutoHoldTM, Reverse mode, and much more. We envisioned all the possible scenarios: a quick grocery run, taking your elderly parents to meet relatives, dropping off your child to school. Of course, safety features like SkidControlTM too, were a top priority. 

Introducing a family-focused scooter in the EV two wheeler sector meant a shift from the usual EV narrative, which often focuses on efficiency or performance. We started our conversation early on, when the Rizta was still under wraps. We wanted to get people thinking about a "family scooter" that fits all their needs. The novelty in messaging and storytelling, led the Rizta to win a significant mindshare for the family scooter position. 

The response has been great. We were clearly able to peak the interest of our TG. Since the last couple of weeks, we’ve been delivering Riztas across different cities and what was great to see was, most customers came with their families and kids to take the delivery of their vehicles. Many customers who already own 450 series scooters, also purchased Rizta scooters for their families. You can very well see in these pictures that our first-time Rizta owners look like they walked right out of a Rizta ad.

The fourth edition of Ather Community Day is here!

The idea behind these community days actually goes back to 2016. Back then, we were a startup without a product. We started Community Meetups to tell our stories and, just as importantly, learn from our owners. Those conversations shaped not just how we talked about Ather Energy, but what we built.

As Ather grew, those meetups grew with us. In 2023, they became the first Ather Community Day, with around 700 people. Last year, nearly 5,000 people joined us. While the scale has changed, the purpose, luckily, hasn't.

Community Day has always been where we share the thinking behind our products. The engineering decisions. The design trade-offs. The details our teams spend months, and often years, obsessing over.

Some of those stories might seem small. In 2024, we spent five minutes on stage talking about a storage box 🤯. Last year, we explained how we reinvented cruise control. Most product launches don't dwell on these details. Most product launches are not aimed at the customer at all. We do, because we believe these are the things that make the experience feel effortless.

This year is a particularly important one for us.

We'll unveil the first scooter built on our all-new EL platform. Our biggest product launch yet.

EL is our first all-new vehicle platform since the original 450. We built it with a simple objective. Bring the Ather experience to a much larger audience without compromising on what makes an Ather an Ather. It's our entry into the mass-market scooter segment and the beginning of the next chapter for Ather.

And EL is just one part of the story. We'll also share what's next across the Ather ecosystem and give everyone a closer look at some of the work happening inside our engineering and R&D teams.

Look forward to meeting you all in Bengaluru on 29th August!

When it came to naming our third R&D facility at Ather Energy, I didn't have to think twice - The Juggernaut. Probably one of the quickest decisions I've made.

Why The Juggernaut? Because the test equipments here are meant to be powerful, relentless and push every vehicle and component to its performance limits.

Building great EVs is an iterative process of designing, breaking and fixing until you are finally satisfied. Doing those iterations at speed is why we built The Juggernaut. 

The focus is simple – Build quality products at Warp speed

With this expansion, we have scaled up testing capability and speed. Eg our new 4 DOF Road Simulator compresses a decade of real-world stress into weeks, helping us find weak links early and fix them faster, and earlier in the development cycle. Multi-stress factor and data-driven testing done in the facility helps us refine the validation processes to improve real-world performance. Additionally, we have added more battery validation tests on  thermal performance, vibration and thermal cycling, IP testing, drop test. Test equipments have been added to do more component tests, hence left shifting the defect discovery in product development cycle.
